paragraphs: In Glasgow the council's own fostering and adoption service is Families for Children, run by Glasgow City Health and Social Care Partnership, and the independent agencies shown above also look for carers in the city. In its May 2025 appeal the council put the number of children living with its foster carers at about 800, and said there is a real need for more people to come forward, both for full-time care and for short breaks.

Short-break carers look after a child for one or two evenings, or a weekend once a month, which many people fit around a job. The council is plain about who can apply: you do not need to be married or own your home, single people and same-sex couples are welcome, and you do not always have to give up work. What you do need is a spare bedroom.

Papers to the city's Integration Joint Board describe the support around carers. A June 2023 report said in-person support groups had restarted with carer champions, and that carers have membership of The Fostering Network, which gives priority access to counselling, financial and legal advice; at a carers' summit that February the partnership counted 394 foster carer households. An update in February 2024 described an online learning platform being set up for carers, life-story training open to every foster carer, and a carers' handbook under review.

Fostering with Families for Children means caring for Glasgow's own children alongside the council's social workers. An independent agency assesses, trains and supports its carers itself, and its carers may be asked to look after children from more than one council. We have not published Glasgow's allowances, so ask the council and two or three of the services above what they pay and what support comes with it. To start with the council, ring 0345 276 5555 or email families.children@sw.glasgow.gov.uk.
Families on the edges of the city can also look at the Renfrewshire, Inverclyde, North Lanarkshire, South Lanarkshire and Scotland pages.
